subject: Biology
title: Keystone Species
description: Learn Keystone Species in one minute.

hook.text: Some species have an outsized impact on their ecosystem. Remove them and everything collapses.

buildup.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins. Without otters, urchins devour kelp forests that shelter thousands.

discovery.text: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995. They changed the behavior of elk herds.

twist.text: With fewer elk grazing riverbanks, trees regrew and rivers actually changed course.

climax.text: Keystone species prove that one organism can shape an entire landscape.

punchline.text: One species can hold a whole ecosystem together.

quiz.question: What happened when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone?
options: Elk behavior changed and rivers shifted

details.summary: Keystone species have a disproportionately large impact on their ecosystem relative to their abundance. Removing a keystone species triggers cascading changes throughout the community, like sea otters whose removal led to urchin explosions that destroyed kelp forests.
details.whyItMatters: Identifying keystone species is critical for conservation because protecting them preserves entire ecosystems. Their outsized influence means that losing one keystone species can collapse communities of hundreds of other species.
takeaways: Sea otters control urchins, preventing kelp forest destruction
Wolves in Yellowstone restored riverbank vegetation through trophic cascades
Keystone species can be predators, herbivores, or ecosystem engineers

faq.question: How do researchers identify a keystone species?
faq.answer: Often through natural experiments where a species disappears and dramatic community changes follow. Controlled removal experiments in intertidal zones first demonstrated the concept. The disproportionate impact relative to biomass is the key criterion.

faq.question: How did wolves change rivers in Yellowstone?
faq.answer: Wolves reduced elk overgrazing on riverbanks, allowing willows and aspens to recover. Stabilized vegetation reduced erosion and changed river channel patterns. This famous trophic cascade showed how one predator can reshape physical landscapes through ecological chains.
